title: Mathematical Foundations of Deep Learning
text:
Preface
The calculus, linear algebra, optimisation and automatic differentiation needed to define, train and analyse feedforward neural networks, presented with proofs at the level of a first graduate course. Out of scope: architectures beyond feedforward networks, statistical learning theory beyond the universal approximation theorem, and implementation details of specific software frameworks.
This textbook is written for readers at the graduate level.

title: Mathematical Foundations of Deep Learning
text:
Conventions

Vectors are bold lowercase column vectors, matrices bold uppercase; the transpose is written with a superscript top.
The gradient of a scalar function is a column vector; the Jacobian of a map has one row per output.
log is the natural logarithm; [P] equals 1 if the statement P holds and 0 otherwise.

title: 1  Calculus
text:
1.1 Derivatives and the chain rule
Training a neural network means minimising a scalar loss over many parameters, and every practical method for that minimisation needs derivatives. This block fixes the basic notions for functions of one real variable; Section 2.1 extends them to several variables.
Equivalently, \(f(a+h) = f(a) + f'(a)\,h + r(h)\) with \(r(h)/h \to 0\) as \(h \to 0\): near \(a\) the function is approximated by an affine map whose slope is the derivative. This first-order view is the one that generalises to many variables and to automatic differentiation.
The auxiliary function \(\varphi\) avoids dividing by \(g(a+h) - g(a)\), which can vanish for arbitrarily small \(h \neq 0\); this is the gap in the tempting argument that simply cancels \(\Delta g\).

title: 1  Calculus
text:
Definition 1.1 (Derivative) Let \(I \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be an open interval and \(f\colon I \to \mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is differentiable at \(a \in I\) if the limit \[
f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}
\tag{1.1}\] exists; the number \(f'(a)\) is the derivative of \(f\) at \(a\).



Theorem 1.1 (Chain rule) Let \(I, J \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) be open intervals, let \(g\colon I \to J\) be differentiable at \(a\) and let \(f\colon J \to \mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \(g(a)\). Then \(f \circ g\) is differentiable at \(a\) and \[
(f\circ g)'(a) = f'\big(g(a)\big)\, g'(a).
\tag{1.2}\]


Proof. Define \(\varphi(y) = \big(f(y) - f(g(a))\big)/\big(y - g(a)\big)\) for \(y \neq g(a)\) and \(\varphi(g(a)) = f'(g(a))\). Differentiability of \(f\) at \(g(a)\) means that \(\varphi\) is continuous at \(g(a)\), and \(f(y) - f(g(a)) = \varphi(y)\,\big(y - g(a)\big)\) holds for every \(y \in J\). Substituting \(y = g(a+h)\) gives \[
\frac{f(g(a+h)) - f(g(a))}{h} = \varphi\big(g(a+h)\big)\,\frac{g(a+h) - g(a)}{h}.
\] As \(h \to 0\) we have \(g(a+h) \to g(a)\) because \(g\) is continuous at \(a\), so the first factor tends to \(f'(g(a))\) and the second to \(g'(a)\).



Example 1.1 (Logistic sigmoid) The logistic sigmoid \(\sigma(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x})\) maps \(\mathbb{R}\) onto \((0,1)\) and is a classical activation function. Writing \(\sigma = f \circ g\) with \(g(x) = 1 + e^{-x}\) and \(f(u) = u^{-1}\), the chain rule gives \(\sigma'(x) = -g(x)^{-2}\cdot(-e^{-x})\), which simplifies to \[
\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)\,\big(1 - \sigma(x)\big).
\tag{1.3}\] Hence \(0 < \sigma'(x) \le \sigma'(0) = 1/4\) for all \(x\); see Figure 1.1. Since the bound is attained only at the origin, a product of many such factors becomes small, which is one reason why deep networks of sigmoid units are hard to train with gradient methods (Goodfellow et al. 2017).







Figure 1.1: The logistic sigmoid \(\sigma\) (solid) and its derivative \(\sigma'\) (dashed); the derivative never exceeds \(1/4\).




Exercise 1.1 Show that \(\tanh(x) = 2\sigma(2x) - 1\) and deduce \(\tanh'(x) = 1 - \tanh^2(x)\) from Equation 1.3 and Theorem 1.1.





Goodfellow, Ian, Yoshua Bengio, Aaron Courville, and Francis Bach. 2017. Deep Learning. MIT Press. http://openlibrary.org/books/OL26455783M/Deep_Learning.

title: 2  Linear Algebra
text:
2.1 Vectors, matrices and gradients
We write vectors as bold lowercase letters and treat them as columns, \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^n\); matrices are bold uppercase, \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), with entries \(A_{ij}\). The transpose turns rows into columns, and the inner product is \(\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{y} = \sum_i x_i y_i\).
For a differentiable \(f\) the expansion \(f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h}) = f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top \mathbf{h} + o(\lVert \mathbf{h}\rVert)\) shows that \(-\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\) is the direction of steepest local decrease, the fact on which gradient descent in Section 3.1 rests. More generally, the Jacobian of \(F\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is the \(m\times n\) matrix \(J_F\) of first partial derivatives, and the multivariate chain rule reads \(J_{F\circ G}(\mathbf{x}) = J_F(G(\mathbf{x}))\,J_G(\mathbf{x})\), the matrix form of Theorem 1.1.

title: 2  Linear Algebra
text:
Proposition 2.1 (Transpose of a product) For \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\) we have \((\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^\top = \mathbf{B}^\top \mathbf{A}^\top\).


Proof. The \((i,j)\) entry of \((\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})^\top\) is the \((j,i)\) entry of \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\), namely \(\sum_{k=1}^n A_{jk} B_{ki}\). The \((i,j)\) entry of \(\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{A}^\top\) is \(\sum_{k=1}^n B_{ki} A_{jk}\), which is the same sum.


Definition 2.1 (Gradient) Let \(U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(f\colon U \to \mathbb{R}\) have all first partial derivatives at \(\mathbf{x}\). The gradient of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{x}\) is the column vector \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \big(\partial f/\partial x_1, \dots, \partial f/\partial x_n\big)^\top\).



Proposition 2.2 (Gradient of a quadratic form) For \(\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and the quadratic form \(q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\) we have \(\nabla q(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A}^\top)\mathbf{x}\); if \(\mathbf{A}\) is symmetric, \(\nabla q(\mathbf{x}) = 2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\).


Proof. Write \(q(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i,j} A_{ij} x_i x_j\). Differentiating with respect to \(x_k\) gives \(\partial q/\partial x_k = \sum_j A_{kj} x_j + \sum_i A_{ik} x_i\), which is the \(k\)-th entry of \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{x}\).


Example 2.1 (Least squares) For a data matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and targets \(\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the loss \(L(\mathbf{w}) = \tfrac12 \lVert \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}\rVert^2\) expands to \(\tfrac12\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} + \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert^2\). Since \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\) is symmetric, Proposition 2.2 gives \[
\nabla L(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}).
\tag{2.1}\] Setting the gradient to zero yields the normal equations \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\), which have a unique solution exactly when \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank.


Exercise 2.1 For \(f(\mathbf{W}) = \operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{W}^\top \mathbf{A})\) with \(\mathbf{W},\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), show that \(\partial f/\partial W_{ij} = A_{ij}\), so that the gradient of \(f\) with respect to the matrix \(\mathbf{W}\) is \(\mathbf{A}\) itself.

title: 3  Optimization
text:
3.1 Gradient descent and convexity
Gradient descent with step size \(\eta>0\) starts from \(\mathbf{x}_0\) and iterates \[
\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k - \eta\,\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k).
\tag{3.1}\] Its analysis rests on a single inequality that bounds how far \(f\) can rise above its linearisation.
Complete arguments are given in (Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004) and, together with stochastic variants, in (Bottou et al. 2018). The rate is sublinear: halving the error requires doubling the number of iterations.
In deep learning the loss is neither convex nor globally smooth, and the gradient is replaced by a stochastic estimate computed on a random mini-batch of training examples (Robbins and Monro 1951; Bottou et al. 2018). The convex theory nevertheless explains the role of the step size and of curvature.

title: 3  Optimization
text:
Definition 3.1 (Convexity and smoothness) A function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex if \(f(\theta\mathbf{x} + (1-\theta)\mathbf{y}) \le \theta f(\mathbf{x}) + (1-\theta) f(\mathbf{y})\) for all \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\). A differentiable \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth if \(\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) - \nabla f(\mathbf{y})\rVert \le L\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\rVert\) for all \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\).



Lemma 3.1 (Descent lemma) If \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth, then \(f(\mathbf{y}) \le f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}) + \tfrac{L}{2}\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\rVert^2\) for all \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\). In particular, one step of Equation 3.1 with \(\eta = 1/L\) satisfies \(f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) \le f(\mathbf{x}_k) - \tfrac{1}{2L}\lVert\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)\rVert^2\).


Proof. Along the segment \(\mathbf{x}+t(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})\), \(t\in[0,1]\), the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(f(\mathbf{y}) - f(\mathbf{x}) - \nabla f(\mathbf{x})^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}) = \int_0^1 \big(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}+t(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})) - \nabla f(\mathbf{x})\big)^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})\,dt\). By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and \(L\)-smoothness the integrand is at most \(tL\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\rVert^2\), and \(\int_0^1 t\,dt = 1/2\). For the second statement substitute \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}_k - \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)/L\).


Theorem 3.1 (Convergence of gradient descent) Let \(f\) be convex and \(L\)-smooth with a minimiser \(\mathbf{x}^\star\). Gradient descent with \(\eta = 1/L\) satisfies \[
f(\mathbf{x}_k) - f(\mathbf{x}^\star) \le \frac{L\,\lVert\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{x}^\star\rVert^2}{2k} \qquad (k\ge 1).
\tag{3.2}\]


Proof. Sketch. Write \(f^\star = f(\mathbf{x}^\star)\). Combining Lemma 3.1 (with \(\eta = 1/L\)) and the convexity inequality \(f^\star \ge f(\mathbf{x}_k) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)^\top(\mathbf{x}^\star - \mathbf{x}_k)\), and expanding \(\lVert\mathbf{x}_{k+1}-\mathbf{x}^\star\rVert^2\) with \(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k - \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)/L\), one obtains \[
f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) - f^\star \le \frac{L}{2}\Big(\lVert\mathbf{x}_k-\mathbf{x}^\star\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf{x}_{k+1}-\mathbf{x}^\star\rVert^2\Big).
\tag{3.3}\] Summing Equation 3.3 from \(0\) to \(k-1\) telescopes the right-hand side to at most \(\tfrac{L}{2}\lVert\mathbf{x}_0-\mathbf{x}^\star\rVert^2\). Since \(f(\mathbf{x}_i)\) is non-increasing by Lemma 3.1, the left-hand side is at least \(k\,\big(f(\mathbf{x}_k) - f^\star\big)\), which gives Equation 3.2.



Example 3.1 (Quadratic model) For \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac12\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{H}\mathbf{x}\) with \(\mathbf{H} = \operatorname{diag}(1, 10)\) we have \(L = 10\), and Equation 3.1 acts coordinate-wise as \(x_{k+1,i} = (1 - \eta h_i)\,x_{k,i}\). With \(\eta = 1/L\) the first coordinate contracts by the factor \(0.9\) per step while the second is annihilated after one step; for \(\eta\) close to \(2/L\) the second coordinate oscillates, and for \(\eta > 2/L\) it diverges. Figure 3.1 shows the stable regimes. The ratio \(10\) between the largest and the smallest curvature, the condition number, governs the speed of convergence.







Figure 3.1: Gradient descent on \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac12(x_1^2 + 10x_2^2)\) from \((-9, 1.5)\) with \(\eta = 0.1 = 1/L\) (solid) and \(\eta = 0.19\) (dashed), shown over level sets of \(f\).





Exercise 3.1 For \(f(x) = \tfrac{a}{2}x^2\) with \(a>0\), show that gradient descent converges for every starting point if and only if \(0 < \eta < 2/a\).





Bottou, Léon, Frank E. Curtis, and Jorge Nocedal. 2018. “Optimization Methods for Large-Scale Machine Learning.” SIAM Review 60 (2): 223–311. https://doi.org/10.1137/16M1080173.


Boyd, Stephen, and Lieven Vandenberghe. 2004. Convex Optimization. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804441.


Robbins, Herbert, and Sutton Monro. 1951. “A Stochastic Approximation Method.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 22 (3): 400–407. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177729586.

title: 4  Automatic Differentiation
text:
4.1 Forward and reverse mode
A program that computes \(f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) from elementary operations defines a computational graph: its nodes are intermediate values \(v_i\), and its edges record which values each operation reads. Automatic differentiation (AD) applies Theorem 1.1 to this graph and produces derivatives that are exact up to floating-point rounding. It differs from finite differences, which suffer from truncation and cancellation errors, and from symbolic differentiation, which can produce very large expressions (Baydin et al. 2015).
This cheap gradient principle is what makes training networks with millions of parameters feasible. Backpropagation, derived in Section 5.1, is reverse-mode AD applied to the loss of a network; forward mode remains preferable when a function has few inputs and many outputs (Baydin et al. 2015).

title: 4  Automatic Differentiation
text:
Example 4.1 (Forward and reverse sweeps by hand) Consider \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1 x_2 + \sin x_1\), evaluated by the trace \[
v_1 = x_1,\quad v_2 = x_2,\quad v_3 = v_1 v_2,\quad v_4 = \sin v_1,\quad v_5 = v_3 + v_4 = f ,
\tag{4.1}\] whose graph is drawn in Figure 4.1.
Forward mode propagates tangents \(\dot v_i = \partial v_i/\partial x_1\) together with the values: \(\dot v_1 = 1\), \(\dot v_2 = 0\), \(\dot v_3 = \dot v_1 v_2 + v_1\dot v_2\), \(\dot v_4 = \cos(v_1)\,\dot v_1\) and \(\dot v_5 = \dot v_3 + \dot v_4\), so that \(\dot v_5 = x_2 + \cos x_1 = \partial f/\partial x_1\). One forward sweep yields one directional derivative, hence the full gradient of a function of \(n\) inputs needs \(n\) sweeps.
Reverse mode first evaluates Equation 4.1 and stores the values, then propagates adjoints \(\bar v_i = \partial f/\partial v_i\) backwards from \(\bar v_5 = 1\): \[
\bar v_3 = \bar v_5,\quad \bar v_4 = \bar v_5,\quad \bar v_1 = \bar v_3\, v_2 + \bar v_4\cos v_1,\quad \bar v_2 = \bar v_3\, v_1 .
\tag{4.2}\] A single reverse sweep therefore returns the whole gradient \(\nabla f = (\bar v_1, \bar v_2)^\top = (x_2 + \cos x_1,\; x_1)^\top\).







Figure 4.1: Computational graph of \(f(x_1,x_2) = x_1x_2 + \sin x_1\). Forward mode follows the arrows; reverse mode sends adjoints against them.




Proposition 4.1 (Cost of reverse mode) For a scalar function evaluated by a program with \(N\) elementary operations, reverse-mode AD computes the full gradient with a number of operations bounded by a small constant multiple of \(N\), independently of the number \(n\) of inputs. The price is memory: the intermediate values of the forward sweep must be stored or recomputed (Griewank and Walther 2008).



Exercise 4.1 Write the evaluation trace and the reverse sweep for \(g(x, y) = e^{xy}/(1 + y^2)\), and check the resulting gradient against direct differentiation.





Baydin, Atilim Gunes, Barak A. Pearlmutter, Alexey Andreyevich Radul, and Jeffrey Mark Siskind. 2015. “Automatic Differentiation in Machine Learning: A Survey.” arXiv:1502.05767. Preprint, arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.05767.


Griewank, Andreas, and Andrea Walther. 2008. Evaluating Derivatives: Principles and Techniques of Algorithmic Differentiation, Second Edition. Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics. https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717761.

title: 5  Neural Networks
text:
5.1 Feedforward networks and backpropagation
In this chapter \(L\) counts layers; it is unrelated to the smoothness constant of Section 3.1. For classification into \(K\) classes the last layer produces scores \(\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^K\), which are turned into probabilities by \(\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_{j} e^{z_j}\) and scored with the cross-entropy \(\ell(\mathbf{z}, y) = -\log\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_y\) of the true class \(y\).
Backpropagation computes all parameter gradients with one reverse sweep, as guaranteed by Proposition 4.1. Writing \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(\ell)} = \partial\ell/\partial\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}\), the chain rule applied to Equation 5.1 gives \[
\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(\ell)} = \Big(\mathbf{W}^{(\ell+1)\top}\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(\ell+1)}\Big)\odot\phi'\big(\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}\big),\qquad
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(\ell)}\,\mathbf{a}^{(\ell-1)\top},\qquad
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}} = \boldsymbol{\delta}^{(\ell)},
\tag{5.2}\] where \(\odot\) denotes the entrywise product and the recursion starts from \(\boldsymbol{\delta}^{(L)} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{e}_y\) by Proposition 5.1. The procedure was popularised for training multilayer networks by Rumelhart et al. (1986), whose experiments showed that hidden units come to represent important features of the task.

title: 5  Neural Networks
text:
Definition 5.1 (Feedforward network) A feedforward network with \(L\) layers maps an input \(\mathbf{a}^{(0)} = \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_0}\) to an output \(\mathbf{a}^{(L)}\) through \[
\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)} = \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{a}^{(\ell-1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(\ell)},\qquad \mathbf{a}^{(\ell)} = \phi\big(\mathbf{z}^{(\ell)}\big),\qquad \ell = 1,\dots,L,
\tag{5.1}\] with weight matrices \(\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_\ell\times n_{\ell-1}}\), bias vectors \(\mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_\ell}\) and an activation function \(\phi\) applied entrywise; in the output layer \(\phi\) is often replaced by the identity or by softmax.



Proposition 5.1 (Gradient of the softmax cross-entropy) With \(\mathbf{p} = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z})\) and \(\mathbf{e}_y\) the \(y\)-th standard basis vector, \(\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}\,\ell = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{e}_y\).


Proof. We have \(\ell = -z_y + \log\sum_j e^{z_j}\). The derivative of the second term with respect to \(z_k\) is \(e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j} = p_k\), and the derivative of \(-z_y\) is \(-1\) if \(k = y\) and \(0\) otherwise.



Example 5.1 (A two-layer network by hand) Take one input \(x\), one hidden unit with weight \(w_1\) and sigmoid activation, one linear output with weight \(w_2\), and the squared loss \(\ell = \tfrac12\big(w_2\,\sigma(w_1 x) - t\big)^2\) for a target \(t\). Then \(\partial\ell/\partial w_2 = \big(w_2\sigma(w_1 x) - t\big)\,\sigma(w_1 x)\) and, using Equation 1.3, \(\partial\ell/\partial w_1 = \big(w_2\sigma(w_1x) - t\big)\,w_2\,\sigma(w_1x)\big(1-\sigma(w_1x)\big)\,x\). These are exactly the two steps of Equation 5.2 for this tiny network.


Exercise 5.1 Check that every product in Equation 5.2 has compatible dimensions, and rewrite the recursion for the activation \(\phi = \tanh\).

title: 5  Neural Networks
text:
5.2 Universal approximation
How expressive are the networks of Definition 5.1? A classical answer concerns networks with a single hidden layer.

Theorem 5.1 (Universal approximation) Let \(\phi\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and sigmoidal, that is, \(\phi(t)\to 1\) as \(t\to\infty\) and \(\phi(t)\to 0\) as \(t\to-\infty\). For every continuous \(f\colon[0,1]^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exist \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), coefficients \(\alpha_j, b_j\in\mathbb{R}\) and vectors \(\mathbf{w}_j\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[
\sup_{\mathbf{x}\in[0,1]^n}\Big|\,f(\mathbf{x}) - \sum_{j=1}^{N}\alpha_j\,\phi\big(\mathbf{w}_j^\top\mathbf{x} + b_j\big)\Big| < \varepsilon .
\tag{5.3}\]

This is Cybenko’s theorem (Cybenko 1989). Hornik (1991) showed that density also holds for every bounded and nonconstant activation, with respect to \(L^p(\mu)\) criteria for finite input measures \(\mu\), so the essential ingredient is the multilayer architecture rather than the particular activation. The logistic sigmoid of Example 1.1 is sigmoidal in the above sense.
The theorem is an existence statement. It gives no bound on the width \(N\) needed for a prescribed \(\varepsilon\), it does not say whether gradient-based training as in Theorem 3.1 finds suitable weights, and it says nothing about generalisation from finite data. Quantitative versions require smoothness assumptions on \(f\), and a satisfactory explanation of why heavily overparameterised networks trained by stochastic gradient descent generalise well is still an open research question (LeCun et al. 2015).

Example 5.2 (Piecewise-linear bumps) With the rectified linear unit \(\operatorname{ReLU}(t) = \max(0,t)\), the combination \(h(t) = \operatorname{ReLU}(t) - 2\operatorname{ReLU}(t - \tfrac12) + \operatorname{ReLU}(t-1)\) is a hat function that vanishes outside \([0,1]\) and peaks at \(h(\tfrac12) = \tfrac12\). Sums of shifted and scaled hats reproduce piecewise-linear interpolation, which converges uniformly to any continuous function on an interval as the mesh is refined: a constructive glimpse of Theorem 5.1 in one dimension, with ReLU in place of a sigmoidal function.


Exercise 5.2 Show that a suitable sum of \(m+1\) hats with nodes \(0, 1/m, \dots, 1\) interpolates \(f\) at the nodes, and bound the uniform error when \(f\) is Lipschitz with constant \(K\).





Cybenko, G. 1989. “Approximation by Superpositions of a Sigmoidal Function.” Mathematics of Control, Signals, and Systems 2 (4): 303–14. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02551274.


Hornik, Kurt. 1991. “Approximation Capabilities of Multilayer Feedforward Networks.” Neural Networks 4 (2): 251–57. https://doi.org/10.1016/0893-6080(91)90009-T.


LeCun, Yann, Yoshua Bengio, and Geoffrey Hinton. 2015. “Deep Learning.” Nature 521 (7553): 436–44. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14539.


Rumelhart, David E., Geoffrey E. Hinton, and Ronald J. Williams. 1986. “Learning Representations by Back-Propagating Errors.” Nature 323 (6088): 533–36. https://doi.org/10.1038/323533a0.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
automatic differentiation

exact-to-rounding evaluation of derivatives by applying the chain rule to a program’s elementary operations (see Section 4.1)

backpropagation

reverse-mode automatic differentiation of a network loss, organised layer by layer (see Section 5.1)

computational graph

the directed graph of intermediate values of a program and the elementary operations that produce them (see Section 4.1)

condition number

the ratio between the largest and the smallest curvature of a quadratic objective (see Section 3.1)

convex function

f(theta x + (1-theta) y) <= theta f(x) + (1-theta) f(y) for all x, y and theta in [0, 1] (see Section 3.1)

cross-entropy

the loss -log p_y of the probability assigned to the true class y (see Section 5.1)

derivative

the limit of the difference quotient (f(a+h) - f(a))/h as h tends to 0, when it exists (see Section 1.1)

differentiable

a function is differentiable at a point if its derivative exists there (see Section 1.1)

feedforward network

a composition of affine maps z = W a + b and entrywise activations a = phi(z), layer by layer (see Section 5.1)

forward mode

automatic differentiation that propagates tangents alongside the values from the inputs to the outputs (see Section 4.1)

gradient

the column vector of first partial derivatives of a scalar function (see Section 2.1)

gradient descent

the iteration x_{k+1} = x_k - eta grad f(x_k) with step size eta > 0 (see Section 3.1)

inner product

for column vectors x and y, the scalar x^T y = sum_i x_i y_i (see Section 2.1)

Jacobian

the m-by-n matrix of first partial derivatives of a map from R^n to R^m (see Section 2.1)

L-smooth function

a differentiable function whose gradient is Lipschitz continuous with constant L (see Section 3.1)

logistic sigmoid

the function sigma(x) = 1/(1 + exp(-x)), mapping the real line onto (0, 1) (see Section 1.1)

quadratic form

a function q(x) = x^T A x for a square matrix A (see Section 2.1)

ReLU

the rectified linear unit t -> max(0, t) (see Section 5.2)

reverse mode

automatic differentiation that propagates adjoints from the output back to the inputs after a forward evaluation (see Section 4.1)

sigmoidal function

a function tending to 1 at plus infinity and to 0 at minus infinity (see Section 5.2)

softmax

the map z -> (e^{z_k} / sum_j e^{z_j})_k from scores to probabilities (see Section 5.1)

universal approximation

the property that one-hidden-layer networks are dense in the continuous functions on a compact set (see Section 5.2)
